source_text: «Ἰσχύσατε, χεῖρες ἀνειμέναι, καὶ γόνατα παραλελυμένα.» Ἐπῃτιᾶτο δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Χριστὸς τοὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων δήμους, ὡς ὀρθὰς μὲν οὐκ ἀνεχομένους ποιεῖσθαι τὰς ἐπ' αὐτῷ τροχιὰς, ἐκτετραμμένας δὲ μᾶλλον εἰς τὸ χωλὸν, καὶ τῶν τῆς ὀρθότητος ἀπολισθήσαντας λογισμῶν. «Υἱοὶ γὰρ,» φησὶν, «ἀλλότριοι ἐψεύσαντό μοι· υἱοὶ ἀλλότριοι ἐπαλαιώθησαν, καὶ ἐχώλαναν ἀπὸ τῶν τρίβων αὐτῶν.» Ἐν ἴσῳ δὴ οὖν ἀλλήλαιν καὶ ἀγχοῦ λίαν, ὡς ἐν ὁμοιότητι παθῶν, χωλότης νοῦ καὶ τυφλότης· ἡ μὲν τὸ ὡς ἐν συνέσει τίμιον, ἡ δὲ τὸ ὡς ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς εὐσθενὲς, εἰς ἀχρειότητα καταφέρουσαι. Ἀπόβλητον δὲ πρὸς τούτοις ὁ νόμος ποιεῖσθαι δεῖν ἔφη τὸν κολοβόρινον, καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ τὸν ὠτότμητον. Ἐφαρμόσειε δ' ἄν τις ἐπ' αὐτοῖς τὸν τοιόνδε λόγον. Αἰσθήσεσι μὲν γὰρ ταῖς ὀσφρητικαῖς τὰ κάκοσμά τε καὶ εὐοσμότατα δοκιμάζεται, τῶν ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν φύσει τοιᾷδε, τῇ τὸ ὀδωδέναι λαχούσῃ, φημί· διακριτικὴ δὲ λίαν ἡ αἴσθησις, καὶ τοῦ κατευφραίνειν εἰδότος, καὶ τοῦ μὴ τοιῶσδε τυχὸν, ἀλλ' ἑτεροίως ἔχοντος, καὶ ὡς ἐν χείρονι μοίρᾳ· νοῦς γε μὴν ἔφη ὁ ἀνθρώπινος, εἰ ἀρτίως ἔχοι τυχὸν ἔν γε τοῖς καθ' ἑαυτὸν, ἴεται μὲν εὐσθενῶς εἰς τὸ διακρίνειν δύνασθαι τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων ποιότητα, ἀκριβῆ δὲ τὴν βάσανον ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ ποιήσεται, καὶ οἷά τις ἄριστος τραπεζίτης δοκιμάζων ἅπαντα, καὶ τὸ μὲν καλὸν κατέχων, καὶ ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδους πονηροῦ ἀπεχόμενος, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον, εὐδοκιμήσει λίαν. Κατακιβδηλεύει γὰρ τὸ οἱονείπως αἰσχρὸν καὶ παράσημον τῶν δρωμένων, προσοῖτο δ' ἂν εὐκόλως τὸ ἐπωφελές τε καὶ ἄμεινον. Οὐκοῦν ἡ σιμότης, τὸ μὴ ἄγαν ὑγιὲς καὶ ἀρτίως ἔχον ὡς ἐν αἰσθήσει δηλοῖ, καθ' ἣν ἕκαστα τῶν πραγμάτων ἄριστα διακρίνοντες, τὴν ἀμείνω μὲν τοῖς ἀρίστοις, τὴν χείρω δὲ τοῖς αἰσχίοσιν ἀπονέμοντες ψῆφον, σοφοί τε καὶ ἀγχίνοοι, καὶ τί γὰρ οὐχὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἐσμέν τε καὶ ὠνομάσμεθα. Ὀσμὴ γὰρ ὥσπερ εἰς νοῦν ἀναθρώσκουσα, τῶν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ νοουμένων οἱονεὶ ποιότης πραγματική. Τὸ δὲ δὴ παρακεκόφθαι τὸ οὖς, ὑπεμφήνειεν ἂν, ὥς γέ μοι δοκεῖ, τὸ δυσήκοον. Παρακεκομμένης γὰρ ἀκοῆς, δοίην ἂν ἔγωγε πάθος εἶναι τὸ ἐκ μέρους εὐπειθὲς, καὶ οὐχ ὁλοκλήρως εὐήνιον εἰς ὑπακοὴν, ἤγουν τὸ μὴ ἀμωμήτως ἐπαΐειν δύνασθαι τῶν ἱερῶν, μάλιστα δὲ γραμμάτων, ὃ δὴ καὶ δρῶσί τινες, ἐφ' ἃ μὴ προσῆκεν ἀβουλότατα παρατρέποντες τῆς ψυχῆς τὸ εὐήκοον. Εἶεν δ' ἂν οὗτοι, κατὰ τὴν τοῦ σοφωτάτου Παύλου φωνὴν, οἱ κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοὴν, καὶ ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς ἀληθείας αὐτὴν ἀποστρέφοντες, προσκείμενοι δὲ πνεύμασι πλάνης, καὶ εἰς βεβήλους κενοφωνίας ἐκνενευκότες. Οὐκοῦν ὁ ὠτότμητος τῆς εἰς τὸ εἴσω καὶ νοητῆς ἀκοῆς ὑπεμφήνειεν ἂν τὴν πήρωσιν, καὶ τὴν ἐξ ὀρθότητος ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον παραφθοράν. Ἀλλὰ καὶ εἴ τῳ τυχὸν σύντριμμα ποδὸς ἢ σύντριμμα χειρὸς ὁρῷτο προσὸν, ἀποχωρείτω, φησὶν, καὶ ἐν ἴσῳ τετάχθω τοῖς ἄλλοις, νοεῖν ἀναπείθοντος τοῦδε τοῦ τὸν πόδα τυχὸν ἢ τὴν χεῖρα συντεθραυσμένου μὲν, πλὴν οὐκ εἰσάπαν ἠῤῥωστηκότος,
pass_a_gloss: [Quote] ‘Be strong (ἰσχύω), slackened (ἀνίημι) hands and paralysed (παραλύω) knees.’ And Christ himself accused (ἐπαιτιάομαι) the peoples of the Jews as not enduring to make the tracks (τροχιαί) toward him straight, but turned (ἐκτρέπω) rather into the lame, and having slipped away (ἀπολισθαίνω) from the reasonings (λογισμοί) of rightness. ‘For foreign sons (υἱοὶ ἀλλότριοι),’ he says, ‘lied to me; foreign sons grew old (παλαιόω) and limped (χωλαίνω) from their paths (τρίβοι).’ Equal to each other and very near, as in likeness of passions, are lameness of mind and blindness: the one [carrying down] the precious in understanding, the other the strong in good works, bringing [them] down to uselessness (ἀχρειότης). Besides these the law said one must make castaway (ἀπόβλητος) the mutilated-nosed and with him the ear-cut. One might fit to them such an account: by the olfactory senses (αἰσθήσεις ὀσφρητικαί) the ill-smelling (κάκοσμα) and most fragrant (εὐοσμότατα) are tested (δοκιμάζω), of things in a nature allotted to have odour (ὄζω); and very discriminating (διακριτική) is the sense, both of what knows to delight (κατευφραίνω) and of what perhaps is not so but otherwise, and as in the worse portion; yet the human mind, he/I said (ἔφη), if perhaps sound in what belongs to it, goes vigorously toward being able to discern the quality (ποιότης) of things, and will make exact assay (βάσανος) of each, and like a best money-changer (τραπεζίτης) testing all, both holding the good and abstaining from every form (εἶδος) of evil, according to what is written, it will be highly approved. For it detects as base coin (κατακιβδηλεύω) what is somehow shameful and falsely stamped (παράσημος) among things done, and would readily accept (προσίεμαι) the profitable and better. So snub-nosedness (σιμότης) shows what is not very healthy and sound as in perception, by which, discerning each thing best, assigning the better vote (ψῆφος) to the best and the worse to the more shameful, we are and are named wise and quick-minded (ἀγχίνοος) and what not of such. For smell, as leaping up into the mind, is as it were the real quality (ποιότης πραγματική) of the things understood by it. To have the ear cut off (παρακόπτω) would hint (ὑπεμφαίνω), it seems to me, the hard-of-hearing (δυσήκοον). For with hearing cut, I would grant the affliction to be the partly obedient (ἐκ μέρους εὐπειθές) and not wholly well-reined (εὐήνιος) toward obedience (ὑπακοή), or the not being able blamelessly to give ear (ἐπαΐω) to the sacred things, especially writings (γράμματα), which some indeed do, most unadvisedly (ἀβουλότατα) turning aside the soul’s good hearing (εὐήκοον) to things not fitting. These would be, by the voice of all-wise Paul, those itched (κνήθω) as to hearing, turning it from the truth, attached (πρόσκειμαι) to spirits of error (πνεύματα πλάνης), and declining (ἐκνεύω) into profane empty-sayings (βέβηλοι κενοφωνίαι). So the ear-cut would hint at the maiming (πήρωσις) of the inward and intelligible hearing, and the corruption from rightness to the worse. But also if perhaps a crushing of foot or of hand is seen present in someone, let him withdraw (ἀποχωρέω), it says, and be ranked equal (ἐν ἴσῳ τάσσω) with the others, this persuading [us] to understand by the one crushed (συνθραύω) perhaps in foot or hand, yet not wholly sick, [cont. §5 τὸν οὐχ ὁλοκλήρως …]
pass_b_english: Cyril: ‘Be strong, you slack hands and paralysed knees’ (Isaiah 35:3). And Christ himself accused the Jewish people of refusing to make their paths toward him straight, letting them turn aside instead into lameness (Hebrews 12:13), and of slipping away from right reasoning. ‘For foreign sons,’ he says, ‘lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped away from their paths’ (Psalm 18:44–45). So lameness of mind and blindness are on a par and very close to each other, being afflictions alike in kind: blindness reduces to uselessness what is precious in understanding, and lameness what is strong in good works. Besides these, the law said that the man with a stunted nose must be rejected, and with him the man with a clipped ear. One might apply to them an explanation like this. By the sense of smell we test what smells foul and what is most fragrant, among things, I mean, whose nature has received the power to give off a smell; and that sense is very discerning, both of what can give delight and of what perhaps is not of that sort but otherwise, ranking, as it were, among the worse. The human mind, I would say, if it is sound in what belongs to it, sets out vigorously to discern the quality of things and will make an exact test of each; and like an excellent money-changer, testing everything, holding fast to what is good and keeping away from every form of evil, as it is written (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22), it will win high approval. For it rejects as counterfeit whatever among our deeds is in any way shameful and falsely stamped, and it would readily accept what is profitable and better. The flattened nose, then, signifies what is not altogether healthy and sound in perception, the faculty by which we discern each thing excellently, give the better verdict to the best and the worse to the more shameful, and are, and are called, wise and quick-witted and everything else of that kind. For the smell, rising as it were to the mind, is the real quality, so to speak, of the things the mind perceives. And to have the ear clipped would suggest, as it seems to me, being hard of hearing. For when the hearing is clipped, I would grant that the affliction is an obedience given only in part, not wholly answering to the rein, or else the inability to listen blamelessly to sacred things, and above all to the sacred writings. Some indeed do just that, most thoughtlessly turning the soul’s readiness to hear toward things it should not. These would be, in the words of the most wise Paul, those who have itching ears and turn their hearing away from the truth (2 Timothy 4:3–4), who devote themselves to spirits of error (1 Timothy 4:1), and who have turned aside to profane, empty talk (1 Timothy 6:20). So the man with a clipped ear would suggest the maiming of the inward and spiritual hearing, and its corruption from rightness into something worse. And if anyone is seen to have a broken foot or a broken hand (Leviticus 21:19), let him withdraw, it says, and be ranked with the others; and here the law leads us to understand, by the man whose foot or hand may have been broken but who is not wholly disabled,

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of Cyril De adoratione Book 12 exists. Translated fresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the earlier English of this book was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; column may cut mid-sentence.

PG 68.788. Isaiah 35:3 is quoted in LXX form (also behind Hebrews 12:12). ‘Make straight paths … lameness … turned aside’ is Hebrews 12:13 (τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιεῖτε … τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ), cited as an allusion in Cyril’s wording, not as Christ’s words; the words Cyril assigns to Christ are the Psalm quotation that follows. Psalm: LXX Psalm 17:45b–46 = English Psalm 18:44b–45. ἡ μὲν … ἡ δὲ resolved by sense (blindness → understanding, lameness → works, as in §3), not by word order. The money-changer image echoes the well-known saying ‘be approved money-changers’ (an unwritten saying, not in the canon), joined here to 1 Thessalonians 5:21–22, which Cyril marks with ‘as it is written’; only 1 Thessalonians is cited. νοῦς γε μὴν ἔφη: ἔφη is odd (perhaps for ἔφην or φημί); rendered ‘I would say’, doubtful reading. κατακιβδηλεύει normally ‘adulterates’; here by context ‘rejects as counterfeit’ (assaying image). ἱερῶν … γραμμάτων ‘sacred writings’ may echo 2 Timothy 3:15 (ἱερὰ γράμματα), a stock phrase: uncited. ‘Spirits of error’: 1 Timothy 4:1 (πνεύμασιν πλάνοις; compare 1 John 4:6), cited 1 Timothy 4:1 since Cyril names Paul; ‘profane empty talk’ also in 2 Timothy 2:16, cited 1 Timothy 6:20 (ἐκτρεπόμενος matches ‘turned aside’). ‘Let him withdraw … same footing as the others’ is Cyril’s paraphrase (φησίν) of the law, not LXX wording; the broken hand/foot is Leviticus 21:19. Ends mid-sentence before §5 τὸν οὐχ ὁλοκλήρως; PG column cut kept.
